stories.title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet
stories.summary: The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage pictured during the party's annual party conference earlier this month

Published 15 September 2026, 00:51 BST

The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.

In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?

And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?

The government is planning to tighten residency rules for people giving money to political parties, to ensure that those making significant donations live in the UK.

But it is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.

Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.

But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to £100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.

But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.

The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published, , external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".

On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons , external that cap would be £100,000 per year. He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.

Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?

And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?

Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.

They have both now returned to the UK.

In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.

But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would be legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.

"Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.

Ah, today, I pointed out.

"Retrospectively declaring donations illegal - that simply cannot be," he pressed on, adding "you cannot confiscate money that has been given legally within the law as it stands."

That is a political, perhaps moral argument, but not a legal one - if the government changes the law, the law of the land will have changed, possibly with consequences for whether those donations are legal.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Farage: Donations to Reform '100% compliant with the law today'

We don't know, because Reform won't tell us, precisely when the two men relocated to the UK. Nor do we know, because the government hasn't decided yet, what relocating - residency - would look like legally.

Would it be being on the electoral roll at a UK address? Would it be being resident in the UK for tax purposes?

The Communities Minister Baroness Taylor told the Lords that Brits returning from abroad and wanting to donate without limit "must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection to the United Kingdom" and the government is "considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy".

In other words the hurdles they plan, while still ill-defined, look like they might be quite high - and folk in government, publicly and privately, are leaning into making that point.

Farage picked a scrap with them in his interview with me, and the government is hitting back.

Do Delo and Harborne clear them, and if they don't, for how long could that delay Reform getting hold of their vast sums of money?

The Reform UK leader has threatened that a Reform government would cut off party funding from the trades unions if the government went ahead with trying to limit his capacity to raise money from these two donors.

Labour received £5m from affiliated unions last year and £12m the year before, in 2024, the year of the last general election.

Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today' Published 19 hours ago

Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall Published 1 day ago

Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change? Published 1 day ago

Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo? Published 3 days ago

So, there are loads of questions that tumble towards us after these donations.

Should there be a limit on the proportion of a party's funding that can come from one individual?

Should there be a limit on what donors based in the UK can give per year, as well as a cap on donations from Brits abroad?

The General Secretary of the Unite union has suggested a domestic cap somewhere between £500,000 and £1m a year. Some argue this would compel parties to find their funding via lots of small donations rather than fewer giant ones. But it could also prompt some to call for state funding of political parties – ie taxpayers picking up the tab – which may not prove wildly popular.

Then there is the question of spending limits, in addition to donation limits, between elections on the top of the existing limits that do apply just before elections.

If I am leaving you with the impression that these donations to Reform, and in particular their scale, are transforming the debates at Westminster about politics and money, well - they are.

And yes, all of the political parties are aware of their own narrow, self interest in all of this - as well as their own sense of the wider good.

stories.summary: New rules introduced on Tuesday mean establishments will be able to accept digital ID apps alongside physical documents.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 September 2026, 00:07 BST

Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

Access concerns

The government wants digital ID apps under its scheme to work together so customers do not need to use different apps in different venues.

It also wants the services to work offline and accessible even without mobile data or a Wi-Fi connection.

In future, the digital proof of age scheme could be extended to cover tobacco and vapes.

But digital rights campaigners have said such measures could lead to the exclusion of some groups.

Jasleen Chaggar of Big Brother Watch said while having multiple ways to prove your identity was helpful, the Government should ensure that digital ID did not become effectively mandatory "as it would shut out millions of people".

"Many people have legitimate reasons for relying on physical ID, whether out of choice, privacy and security concerns, or because they lack the digital skills or means to use digital ID," she said.

"The Government should expressly prohibit businesses from requiring digital IDs for age checks without offering reasonable alternatives," she added.

The new rules come after a wider digital ID programme promoted by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer proved controversial , and was later abandoned by Andy Burnham.

stories.title: Carney gambles on the world's biggest investors betting on Canada
stories.summary: In the midst of a trade war with the US, the prime minister leveraged his connections in global finance to invite some of the world's biggest investors to Canada.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 September 2026

It's been a little over 18 months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country's relationship with the United States, based on over a century of tight economic and military cooperation, was "over".

Trade talks collapsing, tit-for-tat tariffs, and Donald Trump's talk of making Canada a "51st state" have all fuelled this bitter feud between the two North American neighbours.

Now, as Canada's top pitch man, Carney is looking to leverage personal relationships from his time spent in the top tiers of global finance to woo some of the world's wealthiest asset managers and business leaders to bet on his country.

For two days, Toronto will host more than 100 global investors overseeing more than C$100tn ($72tn; £53tn) in assets, in the hope that new economic relationships will help Canada navigate an increasingly unstable geopolitical climate.

On Sunday, at a gala ahead of the summit, the prime minister said the investors "will come to 'peer into our shop window' because the world is looking at Canada differently".

Carney eyes 'unique alliance' with EU as trade war with US intensifies Published 1 day ago

On Monday and Tuesday, a luxury hotel will host guests from major sovereign wealth funds from around the world - including the United Arab Emirates and Norway - and chief executives from major finance companies, like BlackRock's Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.

Carney himself will open the summit on Monday with a private dinner and a keynote address the following morning. Closing the conference will be Stephen Harper, who appointed Carney to lead Canada's central bank during his time as prime minister.

Over roughly 24 hours, Carney hopes to pitch them on Canada's energy and resource sectors, as well as the country’s political stability, in the hopes of getting them to invest in AI, defence, transportation, and infrastructure projects across the country.

It is all part of a strategy to build a "more independent, more resilient economy" in Canada in the wake of the tariff war with the US, which has escalated in recent weeks.

But there is no guarantee that the deep-pocketed investors will be easily sold, and challenges include a track record in Canada of lengthy approvals for projects.

A recent report by the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, which will co-host the summit, cautioned that the scale and depth of investible opportunity is the country's greatest weakness.

"Global capital is looking for opportunity, but opportunity alone does not make a market investible," said Naomi Powell, director of the CPP Investments Insight Institute.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: How much can Canada fight back in its trade war with the US?

While shifting away from its closest business partner will prove a test for Carney, the former central banker has an address book full of the world's biggest business bosses and is on first-name terms with many of them.

"These were personal invites in many cases, literally," said Goldy Hyder, president and chief executive of the Business Council of Canada.

"It's not a group of politicians inviting financiers, it's a group of former financiers and investment people inviting their former buddies," added Miville Tremblay, who worked with Carney for several years at the Bank of Canada, and saw his skills on show during the 2008 global financial crisis.

"He was way above everyone," he said. "He understands finance very deeply. [He] would know when they are bluffing and when the understatement meant that something really bad was happening."

Knowing the minds of investors gives the prime minister, who began his career at investment bank Goldman Sachs, an advantage this week.

Carney is betting his background will boost his country's economic future, though there's little doubt that Canada stands to lose the most from any permanent divorce with the US, the world's largest economy.

Tremblay said Canada seeking investment from overseas was not new, but that the selling pitch to large corporations had now changed.

For the past 25 years, Canada's trade ministers used its proximity to the US as a selling point, pitching to foreign investors that they should "invest in Canada because you've got an easy access to the US market", Tremblay said.

"This line doesn't work anymore."

While the US-Canada trade war rumbles on, many believe there will come a moment when both sides return to the negotiating table.

Bradley Saunders, North America economist for Capital Economics, said securing the future of the trade deal was the "really important thing" for Carney to achieve in the longer term.

"Trade exports to the US are worth 20% of Canada's GDP - that's one of the highest rates in terms of bilateral trade between any two countries in the world.

"If Carney wants to attract long-term investment... he wants this to go well, he has to try and provide a stable environment - and that won't come until Canada has a certain trading relationship with the US."

Tremblay added even if Canada cut its trade with the US over the longer term, it was clear "they'll have to sit down and make a compromise".

Hyder cautioned that investors will want Carney to prove he can fix other barriers to investment, including ensuring indigenous communities and provinces - who have the power to slow or kill major resource projects - are on board with proposals.

Protesters gathered in downtown Toronto on Monday to raise concerns about the possible privatisation of public resources

Tremblay said the pitch has to be "Canada has stuff that the world needs" - which is the exact phrasing Carney has opted for.

Unless a deal was already in the works with another nation, however, he believes it's unlikely any big announcements will be made. He said while overseas investment will be a main aim, encouraging more domestic investment from Canada's largest pension funds, which currently invest more overseas, is also important.

Tremblay added the current tumultuous economic and political climate is perfect for his former boss. "He's a crisis manager. He managed the financial crisis, he managed Brexit, and now he's got a super crisis for Canada."

Carney has been clear that the road ahead for Canada as it pivots away from its reliance on the US will be a tough one.

So far, a majority of Canadians support his course of action, despite some criticism he is turning away from climate commitments as well as towards closer ties with nations like Saudi Arabia and China, as he pushes Canada's rich resources.

There are also protests planned in Toronto on Monday over concerns campaigners say include Ottawa selling the country to corporate interests.

Still, Drew Fagan, a professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs, says the main challenge for the prime minister is the current rift with the US happening more rapidly than the time it takes to develop and build new global trade partnerships.

"And in the interim, that's where the valley of death is for him, both economically and potentially politically," he said.

stories.title: Burnham cancels engagements after death of father
stories.summary: Burnham has previously said his father did not know he had become prime minister due to his Alzheimer's.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Burnham pictured with his parents, Eileen and Roy, after he was selected as Labour's candidate to become the mayor of Greater Manchester in 2016

Published 14 September 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England .

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Burnham told the BBC that while his father could not be there when he entered No 10 to take up the role, he and his mother had "exchanged a few words about my dad and how proud he would be".

"That's a little hard, but then again I've said, it's their achievement", he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg in July.

"The emotion of that moment was, well, bittersweet - it was painful in one way but beautiful in another."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

stories.title: Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today'
stories.summary: Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 September 2026

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said two big donations given to his party are "100% compliant with the law today", but was not able say whether they would be permissible if a rule change, currently being debated in Parliament, were passed.

Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026.

Farage argued the government should not retrospectively declare donations illegal and threatened to retaliate by limiting trade union donations, if elected PM.

Trade union leader Paul Nowak said there was no similarity between "care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires."

Over the weekend, Reform announced that it had received two donations of £36m each from wealthy businessmen Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British but have until recently lived abroad.

Speaking to the BBC, Farage said there was "no question" their donations - the largest in British political history - were within the law "as it stands".

Asked if the two men were resident in the UK by 25 March, Farage said: "I'm not going into their particular details."

He went on to criticise the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal, saying: "This cannot be."

"If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall Published 1 day ago

Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change? Published 1 day ago

Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo? Published 3 days ago

On Monday the House of Lords debated the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at £100,000.

The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than £100,000.

The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters".

She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.

The two £36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas.

"I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said.

He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that."

Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise".

He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages".

By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election.

Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense".

He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency.

Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference.

TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy".

Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap between £500,000 and £1m on individual donations made by UK residents

Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap".

stories.title: Farm tax a mistake, Lord Blunkett says in call for Burnham 'rural reset'
stories.summary: The former mentor to Prime Minister Andy Burnham has joined ex-PM Lord Cameron in criticising rural policies.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lord Blunkett spoke at a countryside campaigning event in central London

Published 14 September 2026

An inheritance tax for farms was "a mistake" and Andy Burnham should use his premiership to listen to the countryside more, his longtime mentor Lord Blunkett has said.

The former Labour minister hit out at "Treasury economic orthodoxy" over the 20% tax on inherited agricultural assets worth more than £2.5m that came into force in April, ending a waiver farms had since the 1980s.

He spoke at the launch of a new campaign by the Countryside Alliance for a "rural reset" to reverse what the group says is a current set of policies "treating rural people as the enemy".

The government said it was "determined to rebuild trust" with farmers and that most estates were unaffected by the tax hike.

The tax, announced in last year's Budget under Sir Keir Starmer at half the 40% rate of standard inheritance tax, was initially proposed for inherited agricultural assets worth more than £1m.

A backlash led to it being watered down in December - to a raised threshold of £2.5m.

Some rural campaigners say this still impacts ordinary working family farms and are calling for it to be scrapped.

'Touched a nerve'

Burnham has not hinted any change or U-turn on the issue, but Lord Blunkett said he was confident the now-prime minister, who he hired as his parliamentary private secretary back in 2004, would get the message "very clearly and act accordingly".

"I think the family tax, the family farm imposition, was a mistake," the former Labour minister said, adding it "touched a nerve".

"It's very strange because we've never won so many rural seats since 1945 - around 135 Labour MPs are either rural or semi-rural - and their voices need to be heard much more clearly," he told the BBC.

"If you're an urban dweller all your life and you've got Treasury economic orthodoxy in your soul, you won't understand that family farms are only family because they are passed down from one generation to another."

He said the countryside fits neatly into Burnham's self-professed focus on local postcodes and urban and rural areas "need each other".

Lord Blunkett also branded the government's planned ban on trail hunting a mistake, saying the practice was "doing no harm".

Farmers have held tractor protests in London and elsewhere over the last year

Trail hunting was introduced after the Hunting Act 2004 as an alternative to hounds chasing foxes and involves using an animal-scented rag. Labour first announced a planned ban in its 2024 election manifesto.

The government said there was strong support for a ban on trail hunting and that it posed risks to wildlife and pets.

Former Prime Minister Lord Cameron criticised both policies at a Countryside Alliance event in Westminster on Monday, calling the inheritance tax on farm assets "stupid" and the trail hunting ban "completely wrong".

Also taking aim at the government's call for evidence on game shooting in England, Lord Cameron warned further crackdowns risk eroding all facets of rural life including pubs and local services.

"Some of these things we should be angry about," he added, a week after being spotted filming an episode of Prime series Clarkson's Farm which has popularised various issues facing farmers.

The Countryside Alliance says its campaign is a non-political effort to encourage Burnham to work with rural people to address their concerns about policies on issues like farming, horseracing and greyhound racing.

Farmers have held tractor protests in parts of the country over the last year.

The government said: "This is the start of a new conversation with farmers and rural communities as we work together to build a stronger future for British farming and unlock growth in rural areas."

stories.title: Former top civil servant received pay-off of nearly £860,000
stories.summary: Lord Wormald became the shortest-serving cabinet secretary in the history of the post when he left in February.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 September 2026

A former top civil servant received a record pay-off of nearly £860,000 after he was forced out of his job by Sir Keir Starmer, just 14 months after the then-prime minister appointed him.

Lord Wormald left his role as cabinet secretary and head of the Civil Service in February by "mutual agreement" following months of media reports suggesting Downing Street was unhappy with his performance.

The Cabinet Office's accounts , external show there was "contractual compensation" of £332,897 and "additional severance" of £526,598.

The BBC understands the size of the pay-off was partly to cover Lord Wormald's pension contributions as his removal from office essentially cut his civil service career short.

He also was compensated for a mandatory "waiting period" following his departure from government. As cabinet secretary he would have had regular access to sensitive information about national security, foreign policy and the UK economy.

His salary for the period 1 April 2025 to 13 February was between £210,000 and £215,000, according to the accounts, bringing his total for the year to more than £1m.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson said: "We do not comment on HR matters.

"The permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office received a ministerial direction from the then-prime minister to proceed with the payment to the former cabinet secretary. Their exchange of letters is a matter of public record."

The accounts state Sir Keir authorised the "special severance package" on 16 February.

A note in them also states: "The former cabinet secretary elected to take early payment of his pension.

"The majority of the total severance payment was used to ensure he could access the full value of his pension that would have been due at normal retirement age, rather than it being reduced for early payment."

The BBC has approached Lord Wormald and Sir Keir for comment.

Conservative shadow Cabinet Office minister Alex Burghart said: "Chris Wormald was just one of many civil servants and advisers fired by Keir Starmer as he tried to save his own skin.

"This payout is another appalling waste of taxpayers' money by Labour."

The UK's top civil servant sits next to the prime minister during cabinet minister meetings, which usually take place weekly in Downing Street when Parliament is sitting.

They are responsible for ensuring policy decisions are put into action and are ultimately responsible for all civil servants in Great Britain.

At the time of his appointment in December 2024, Sir Keir said Lord Wormald would be tasked with "the complete re-wiring of the British state to deliver bold and ambitious long-term reform".

As a career civil servant, some questioned whether he was the best person to reform the Civil Service.

Lord Wormald was replaced in February, making him the shortest-serving cabinet secretary in the history of the post.

The FDA Union, which represents senior civil servants, responded to his departure by criticising "anonymous briefings" against him and called his treatment "a new low for this government and its relationship with the Civil Service".

Lord Wormald was replaced by Dame Antonia Romeo .

He was later given a seat in the House of Lords in one of Sir Keir's last acts as prime minister.

Lord Wormald will be an independent crossbench peer and is scheduled to formally take his seat on Thursday.

stories.title: Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say
stories.summary: The leaders of Plaid Cymru, SNP and Sinn Fein say the UK government should prepare for constitutional change.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth, Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O'Neill met in Cardiff Bay on Monday

Published 13 September 2026

The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

The nationalist leaders from Plaid Cymru, Sinn Féin and the SNP - who want their countries to leave the United Kingdom - signed an agreement on Monday which said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

But while Scotland's John Swinney and Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill called for referendums at a joint press conference, Wales' Rhun ap Iorwerth declined to give a timetable for one in his country.

Labour and Reform accused Plaid of wanting to break up the UK.

Swinney and ap Iorwerth's governments later backed a separate agreement agreed to work together on pressing UK government on "fairness" in funding and powers.

For the first time since devolution began, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.

All three met on Monday as representatives of their parties. Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald also attended.

The memorandum of understanding said: "For people watching across these islands - for people watching around the world - there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end.

"No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.

"We recognise that our parties have different constitutional positions and that each nation will determine its own future in its own way and in its own time."

'Pivotal moment' as Swinney attends leaders summit Published 1 day ago

Little-Pengelly criticises O'Neill as nationalist first ministers to meet Published 1 day ago

Plaid has ruled out an independence referendum before the next Senedd election in 2030.

At the press conference, ap Iorwerth said there was a "growing recognition that Westminster is not working" and "power genuinely needs to be brought closer to people and communities".

He said the May Senedd election gave his government "a mandate for change to make Wales more confident, more prosperous and more in control of its future".

"Wales should have the power, the resources, the fair treatment we need as a nation to build the future our people deserve," he said.

SNP leader Swinney said Monday was a "pivotal moment in the constitutional journey of the United Kingdom".

He said the elections in May for each nation created a situation with first ministers who believe "their countries should decide their own future".

"That principle of self-determination is an inalienable right," he said.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Rhun ap Iorwerth says it is "up to the people of Wales to decide their own future"

He described Andy Burnham as the "last prime minister of the United Kingdom".

"Because the people of Scotland, if given the choice of independence in a referendum will take that choice."

Sinn Féin's McDonald described Monday's meeting as "historic", saying: "We have the right to referendum. We have the right to decide our future.

"We will not accept or tolerate any prime minister telling us that right is off the table."

Northern Ireland's First Minister O'Neill said all three nations were "distinctively different" and had their own priorities.

But she said the "common cause here is that Westminster does not and will never serve our people well".

O'Neill serves in a power sharing executive in Northern Ireland, where the Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) deputy first minister Emma Little-Pengelly accused the Sinn Fein politician of attempting to "weaponise the role of first minister" .

In Northern Ireland, the first and deputy first minister have identical powers .

The leaders signed an agreement which said each nation will determine its own future "in its own way and in its own time"

Asked by BBC Wales to clarify what the memorandum of understanding meant for Wales, and whether it meant asking Westminster not to block a Welsh independence referendum, ap Iorwerth said it was "up to the people of Wales to decide its own future".

Pressed further, he said: "The timescale will be set by the people of Wales when they are persuaded. My job is to persuade."

The Welsh government does not have the power to hold such a referendum, but ap Iorwerth told the press conference he wanted to see that devolved.

Later on Monday, Swinney and ap Iorwerth signed an agreement between the Welsh and Scottish governments.

The agreement, which is not legally binding, said it would "press the case for greater fairness for Wales and Scotland in areas such as the operation of the UK funding arrangements and powers over our constitutional future".

It said the two governments would work together on a range of issues, including tackling child poverty and maximising the benefits of their relationships with the European Union.

The first ministers of Wales and Scotland signed a co-operation agreement between their two nations on Monday afternoon

At a second press conference, Swinney declined to offer support for reform of the Barnett Formula - the system that determines how Wales is funded.

Welsh ministers have long called for the Barnett funding formula to be reformed, claiming it disadvantages Wales.

However, it is argued Scotland does well from the formula.

Before he became prime minister, Burnham made the case for change, but on his recent visit to Wales he played down the prospect of reform.

Swinney said: "Financial arrangements across the United Kingdom vary and by constituent part of the United Kingdom. We all have to put forward the issues and the interests and the perspectives in each of our countries."

Ap Iorwerth said: "There are flexibilities that Scotland already have right now as a minimum to be handed to Wales, is something that is important to us."

Walescast: Is Westminster's Time Coming to an End?

For the first time since devolution began, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland are all led by first ministers who support leaving the United Kingdom.

During Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Burnham appeared to indicate a second referendum could be held in Scotland if there was clear public support for a vote.

He compared the situation to the conditions for a border poll in Northern Ireland, explaining the Good Friday Agreement made clear a poll would be "considered by the Northern Ireland secretary when there is a clear consensus in the country, when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered".

"I would say that it is exactly the same situation in Scotland," he added.

The apparent softening in tone was welcomed by Swinney before Burnham clarified that another Scottish referendum remained "off limits" .

A referendum on Scottish independence in September 2014 saw the country vote to remain part of the UK by a margin of 55% to 45%.

Andy Burnham will meet the devolved leaders next month

The dynamics in Wales are different from those in Scotland.

Ap Iorwerth, who was appointed the first non-Labour first minister of Wales after May's Senedd election, had ruled out pushing for a referendum on Welsh independence during his party's first term in government.

His government intends to set up a national commission to "lay the foundations" for future plans for Welsh independence.

In the meantime, Welsh ministers are seeking extra powers to be transferred to Wales, including over policing and youth justice - which Burnham has said he is "open" to the idea of .

Ap Iorwerth said Burnham had "a lot to learn" about "how devolution to a nation is rather different to devolution to a region or a city of England".

"I want to have a positive relationship with him, I believe he wants to have a positive relationship with me," he said.

The UK government said: "The prime minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the union."

The devolved leaders will meet the prime minister next month.

Labour leader in Wales, Ken Skates, said: "Plaid have given people nothing since the election.

"They clearly want to use power to break up Britain, weaken Wales and spend their time obsessing over more powers for their politicians."

Welsh Conservative Senedd leader Darren Millar said: "Instead of obsessing about independence, the first minister should be focused on dealing with the crisis engulfing the Welsh NHS and the declining standards in Welsh schools."

Dan Thomas, Reform UK's Welsh leader, said: "The first minister can't get a grip of NHS waiting lists or our education system, but apparently has time to tell us what we all know. That he wants the break up the UK."

stories.title: 'Culture shift' needed in how UK does business, PM urges
stories.summary: Burnham says those who take risks should be backed by government, but his government has been criticised for increasing business costs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 13 September 2026

The UK needs a "culture shift" in how it does business, Andy Burnham has said ahead of a meeting between some of Britain's biggest bosses and the government.

The prime minister said those who take risks in business should be backed by government and local leaders should have the power to work with companies.

Burnham had been due to attend the meeting, but cancelled his engagements for Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father.

The Labour government has been criticised for increasing costs for firms, such as with the employer national insurance and minimum wage changes under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The meeting comes as Chancellor John Healey prepares for his first Budget next month, with rising borrowing costs in recent weeks adding to the pressure on government finances.

Monday's gathering will include the heads of companies such as BP, Shell, HSBC, Morrisons, Sainsbury's, BT, Vodafone and Rolls-Royce.

Ahead of the meeting, Burnham said he would give people "the confidence that if they have a great idea, they'll get all the support they need to bring it to life".

"When local leaders have the tools to get things done and government works in partnership with business, you can pull in investment, create jobs and transform communities," he said.

He added the government would be "a partner for growth to make every part of Britain better off".

The meeting comes as higher borrowing costs in the UK and other countries present problems for governments looking to spend money on business support or investment.

Separately, hundreds of hospitality businesses have written to the prime minister , external , calling on him to cut VAT for the sector.

More than 800 pub, restaurant and hotel bosses - include celebrity chefs Heston Blumenthal and Tom Kerridge - signed the letter asking for the hospitality VAT rate to be reduced from 20% to 10%.

When he was still Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said he would argue for the tax to be in line with the lower rates seen in other European countries.

AI boom helps drive surprise UK growth in July Published 4 days ago

Why are petrol and diesel prices rising again? Published 1 day ago

Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night Published 2 September

Official data revealed a surprise boost in the economy in July partly driven by artificial intelligence (AI) investment , though experts expect growth to slow in the months ahead due to high energy prices.

The US-Israel war with Iran has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices , affecting households and businesses.

The rise in energy costs has prompted fears that inflation will remain high and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep the pace of price rises under control.

The expectation of higher interest rates, as well as competition in the global debt market from AI firms looking to spend money on development, has driven up the cost of government borrowing in many countries.

However, many argue the UK has a particular problem. The UK yield for 10-year bonds, a key measure of government debt costs, is higher than countries such as the US, France, and Japan.

Experts say this is due to several factors affecting investor confidence in the UK, such as multiple prime ministers, chancellors and policy U-turns over a short period.

The boss of chip designer Fractile, Walter Goodwin, who will be attending the meeting on Monday, said the government's acknowledgement that high-growth businesses are crucial to job creation and the economy has been "a positive thing".

But speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said the UK could do better in attracting the best talent as the current system is "less dynamic" than other countries.

Goodwin said the UK should be attracting the best talent in the world, and mobility could be improved by reducing notice periods for when someone wants to change jobs from three months to a shorter timescale.

In an interview with the BBC last week, Healey called for a restoration of "confidence about Britain" despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs .

Others have argued that the Labour government has created its own problems by increasing costs for businesses.

Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "The way for the prime minister to get businesses thriving, delivering jobs and driving growth is to cut their taxes.

"Labour's jobs tax and employer red tape have been devastating for businesses. The consequence has been a drying-up of the jobs market, weaker investment and businesses facing ever greater costs."

Prime minister vows to ‘reindustrialise Britain’ through new partnership with business

The prime minister is to host business leaders, entrepreneurs and local mayors at Downing Street on Monday to pitch his government as a “partner for growth” that can offer a stable platform for investment and jobs in the UK.

Ahead of the event, Andy Burnham said the country had “everything it needs to succeed”, including talented people and world-class universities, but requires “a culture shift in how Britain does business” if it is to unlock its full potential.

The new prime minister vowed to “reindustrialise Britain” through a new partnership with business. “That means putting government firmly on the side of the people who take risks, start companies, create jobs and bring new ideas to life,” he said.

“It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life.”

Burnham will host a roundtable with entrepreneurs – including the founders of Octopus Energy, Revolut and Starling Bank and quantum computing companies including Oxford Quantum Circuits – before welcoming chief executives from some of Britain’s largest businesses for a reception in No 10 along with regional mayors.

They include the bosses of financial companies HSBC, Aviva and Standard Chartered, supermarkets Morrisons and Sainsbury’s, telecoms groups BT and Vodafone, oil companies BP and Shell and manufacturers Rolls-Royce and BAE Systems.

Monday’s round of meetings come as Burnham and John Healey , the chancellor, prepare for their first budget on 28 October.

Burnham has vowed to deliver growth across the country and to devolve power and resources away from Westminster to do so. But Healey faces a tough task, presenting his budget amid rising borrowing costs and the impact of the Iran war on the global economy.

Although the economy unexpectedly grew by 0.4% in July , boosted by AI and cloud computing, economists have warned rising energy costs may have held back growth in August and September.

Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants England and Wales, said the chancellor could be left with a “budget headache” if economic growth starts to dwindle, as more muted growth and surging borrowing costs erode his fiscal headroom, raising the prospect of further tax rises.

Both Burnham and Healey have stressed their commitment to the fiscal rules laid down by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, which require day-to-day spending to be covered by taxes and government debt to fall as a share of the economy by 2029/30. They are also bound by Labour’s manifesto commitment not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.

In his first major speech as chancellor last week, Healey said boosting economic growth would be his defining mission as chancellor but also warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.

He talked of putting more power and resources into the hands of local leaders, reducing the cost of doing business and using public investment to attract private capital.

stories.summary: The former UK PM said: "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning".

Watch: Why Russian strike on train near Ukraine-Poland border could mark an escalation

Published 13 September 2026

A Russian drone has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through.

No casualties were reported after the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. All the passengers had been evacuated, Ukrainian authorities said.

Johnson and other European national security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on a different train on their way back from a conference in Kyiv.

Russia's defence ministry said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train".

PM's top security adviser says Europe faces hard winter to keep pressure on Putin Published 2 days ago

Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches Published 5 days ago

Professor Katarzyna Pisarska, chair of the Warsaw Security Forum, told the BBC she was in the same carriage as Johnson and Powell, and the attack had happened about 30 minutes after their train had crossed into the Polish border.

In a statement, Ukraine's railway authority Ukrzaliznytsia said the diplomatic train "had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes".

It also said that an evacuation order for passengers on the hit train had been given "just 15 minutes" before the strike by a Russian jet-propelled drone.

Former CIA chief David Petraeus, who had been on board another train at Yahodyn station at the time of the strike, said the incident was "terrifying".

In an interview with the New York Times, Petraeus said: "This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorise Ukrainian civilians."

Both Ukrainian and Polish authorities said the Russian drone had struck 2km (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Moment Russian strike hits near Ukraine-Poland border

Johnson wrote on X: "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning.

He said this was "the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day - even on civilian railways" and urged Kyiv's allies to urgently provide Ukrainians "the air defences they need".

Ukraine has made repeated pleas to its allies - particularly the US - to provide more interceptors to defend against daily Russian attacks that increasingly use fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-propelled drones.

Johnson, seen here at a book fair in Lviv last week, was on the train alongside top European security officials

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric strikes" at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn amounted to "[Russian President Vladimir] Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and Nato" and renewed calls for more sanctions on Moscow.

In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk held an emergency meeting to discuss the latest developments, saying that Russian actions were "getting closer and closer to our border."

Meanwhile, the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Russia of attempting to scare Western countries with the attack.

In response to a question about the incident, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday: "Our military has been conducting operations across the entire territory of Ukraine and will continue to do so."

Johnson and other top European security advisers were on their way back from the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv - an annual event that brings together leaders and experts from politics, business, security and mass media.

Ukraine said strikes had continued overnight, with the country's air force reporting that 85 of 108 Russian drones that were launched had been shot down.

Police in Chernihiv said on Monday morning that three people had died after a warehouse belonging to an agricultural business was struck in Pryluky.

Russia's defence ministry also reported that nearly 400 Ukrainian drones had been destroyed over Russian regions overnight.

Russia appears to be escalating its war against Ukraine by targeting trains, railway depots, petrol stations and border crossings.

Earlier this week, two people were killed when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

Also this week, a female conductor died in a Russian drone attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine. Six Ukrzaliznytsia employees were killed after a depot was struck in Kyiv at the start of the month.

In January, Zelensky condemned as "terrorism" a Russian strike on a crowded passenger train in the north-eastern Kharkiv region that left five people dead.

The Russian attacks have significantly damaged Ukraine's vast train network - the main mode of transportation for millions of Ukrainians as all air travel has been suspended since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

European countries are also blaming Russia for suspicious incidents on their territory.

Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd".

There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.

Russian authorities have also accused Ukraine of targeting trains and busses in recent months.

Last year, Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said it targeted a railway bridge in Crimea following an operation lasting "several months".

The Crimea bridge - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the Crimean Peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018.

stories.title: Campaigners told to respect rivals as local election abuse rises
stories.summary: A survey suggests more than half of candidates in the May 2026 polls in England faced harassment or intimidation.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Local elections were held in England earlier this year across 5,000 seats,136 councils and six mayoralties

Published 14 September 2026

Political parties should require members to respect one another during elections, the Electoral Commission has said after finding rising levels of abuse.

More than half of candidates in the May 2026 English local and mayoral polls experienced a problem with harassment or intimidation, the highest level over the last four years, according to its survey of 25,000 who stood.

A report , external published on Monday said such issues were most likely to affect women, people from ethnic minority backgrounds and those with a disability.

The watchdog is calling on political parties to make clear in their own rules that members "must respect other campaigners", with potential disciplinary action if they do not.

The report also recommended requiring social media companies to improve protections for electoral candidates online, including rapidly removing abusive content and identifying perpetrators.

Inappropriate contact through social media was the most frequently experienced scenario of harassment or abuse for local candidates, the survey found, with disinformation through generative AI also flagged as an issue.

One candidate told the survey their daughter had "called me from school crying" because she had seen posts online branding them "racist, fascist and Nazi".

Another candidate reported being screamed at with death threats while leafleting on doorsteps, but could not run away because of their disability.

Reform UK and Labour candidates were more than twice as likely as Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to say they had experienced such issues in the May 2026 elections in England , with the Greens and independents between both groups.

Some 79% of female respondents reported avoiding the campaign trail on their own at least once, compared to just under half of male counterparts. One female candidate said they felt the need to bring their husband with them.

And a third of respondents overall considered not standing for election because of harassment, intimidation or concerns about future abuse.

Only 15% of those surveyed had reported such experiences to the police.

"These elections demonstrate the growing threats posed to democracy," the Electoral Commission's chief executive Vijay Rangarajan said.

He added: "Without improvements to candidate safety, there is a significant risk that people will be put off standing in future elections."

stories.title: Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall
stories.summary: The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Nigel Farage's party has accused Labour of trying to "rig the system"

Published 14 September 2026

The House of Lords will debate changes to the laws on political donations later on Monday after Reform UK received £72m from two billionaires in 24 hours.

Calls for restrictions are growing after huge donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.

The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

The leader of one of Labour's biggest funders, Unite the Union, is among those backing limits on individual donations. In response, Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice said the proposed change shows Labour was "terrified" of the party.

"We believe that we've done everything in complete accordance with the laws," he told BBC Breakfast.

He accused Labour of trying to "retrospectively introduce legislation in order to significantly disadvantage another political party".

Tice said the party's donations would enable it to "get on a level playing field" with other parties, likened it to Labour receiving donations from trade unions, and that "competition is a good thing".

But Paul Nowak, the leader of Britain's trade unionists in his role as TUC general secretary, rejected comparisons between donations from wealthy individuals and unions.

Speaking at the TUC's annual congress in Brighton on Monday, Nowak said: "Let no-one tell you there is any similarity between care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires."

He added a "proper conversation about how we clean up our politics" is required.

The sheer scale of Reform's record-breaking donation windfall has prompted an urgent debate across the parties.

On Monday, the bill that would introduce a £100,000 cap on donations from British voters living abroad returns to the House of Lords.

The rules were proposed in a review by former civil servant Philip Rycroft aimed at countering foreign influence in UK politics.

The self-described entrepreneur and philanthropist, Ben Delo, made headlines over the weekend with a record-breaking £36m donation to Reform UK.

The Labour peer Lord Wills told Radio 4's Westminster Hour he intended to amend the bill so that donations from those living in the UK could also be capped.

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, also told the BBC a limit on individual donations was necessary.

Her union has donated large sums to Labour in recent years, but she argues that "billionaires splashing out millions" is different from "everyday workers giving 10p a week to a political fund".

Reform have said "Labour and their union pals know they can't win an election fairly so now they want to rig the system".

Questions remain over whether Reform will be able to keep all of the £72m.

Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, told the BBC on Sunday the donations were "entirely in line with the law as it is, and as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future".

The government has also proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.

This would be in place for the rest of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".

Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she did not "understand" their "circumstances".

The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong.

BBC News has been told both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.

The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.

stories.title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights
stories.summary: Existing laws are not equipped to address the risks to human rights being posed by artificial intelligence, UK politicians say.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 September 2026

A cross-party group of MPs and peers has identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI), arguing existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.

The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

"Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," said Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel.

Labour education minister Georgia Gould said AI was creating opportunities but that it was critical the government was "responding to those risks" posed by the technology.

In a summary of its 100-page report, the JCHR argued AI has been responsible for numerous abuses of human rights, citing examples including the use of AI to create sexualised images of women and girls, and scanning people's faces without their consent.

The JCHR has advocated for the creation of a "single, independent AI oversight body... on a statutory basis", saying the current legal framework is "fragmented and difficult to navigate", "leaving gaps in protection".

The report goes on to call for "more demanding obligations for higher risk AI systems and models" at all stages of the "AI lifecycle".

It continues: "Some uses of AI should be prohibited outright because they are incompatible with human rights. Potential areas for action include subliminal techniques, and inappropriate use of profiling or biometric data."

The committee's chair said: "AI is heralded as an unprecedented era of technological development with the potential to transform our lives for better or for worse."

"It is moving with such speed and complexity that its impact is hard to accurately predict. What is clear is that at present we are unprepared to deal with its consequences however potentially dire they may be."

The JCHR's 12 members are drawn from both Houses of Parliament and they currently include MPs and peers from the Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties.

Monday's report comes amid growing anxiety over the challenges posed by AI.

Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who quit Anthropic, told the BBC this weekend that staff developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity .

An Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News that it was building "models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry".

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto said it would "ensure the safe development and use of AI models by introducing binding regulation on the handful of companies developing the most powerful AI models".

The government used the King's Speech in July 2024 to commit to bringing forward "appropriate legislation", but no dedicated AI bill appeared in this year's King's Speech.

Asked what had happened to the law promised by Labour, Gould told BBC Breakfast that the government "has been regulating" - including action to tackle non-consensual sexualised deepfakes and a bill linked to cyber security.

She said: "There is action happening and we're continuing to really carefully monitor the rise of AI, the way the technology is evolving and making sure we're staying alongside it, and we have some of the best people in the world doing that work."

Gould said the AI Security Institute was "working through challenges coming in the future, testing models when they're coming into the UK", and that there was a need to work with other countries on the issue.

Following his arrival in No 10 in July, Prime Minister Andy Burnham ensured AI Minister Kanishka Narayan would attend cabinet meetings after scrapping the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and splitting its responsibilities among other government departments.

On Saturday, the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, proposed a plan calling for the regulation of AI.

Amodei's plan included global regulation, industry-wide regulation and independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed.

He also urged the pace of development to be slowed down and the bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, said they agreed with him.

One human rights concern raised in recent years is that AI can display biases against particular groups if trained on large datasets scraped from the internet which can include racist, sexist and other undesirable material.

stories.title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England
stories.summary: The government describes its new school food standards as "once-in-a-generation changes".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 13 September 2026

There will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the government has called the biggest shake-up to school dinners in England in over a decade.

Under new school food standards, fibre and wholegrains will also be increased, and breakfast clubs will have to follow nutrition rules for the first time, with schools also being monitored.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) welcomed the changes, but said they hoped the new rules would not become "another stick with which to beat head teachers".

The changes will come into effect from 2027 and be funded with existing money for schools, the government said.

As part of the new framework, sweet desserts, like cake, will be reduced from a regular lunch offer to twice a week in secondary schools, and once a week in primary schools. They also must now be served with a portion of fruit.

Servings of processed meats such as ham, sausages and chicken nuggets have been reduced to once a week and must come with a side of vegetables or fruit.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said they were "once-in-a-generation changes" which would "transform school food for children across the country".

The Department for Education said it hoped the reforms would tackle childhood obesity, improve nutrition and support children's concentration, learning and wellbeing.

Schools will be required to publish food policies and menus online with monitoring arrangements set to be developed alongside the Food Standards Agency, it said.

Pepe Di'Iasio, ASCL general secretary, said parents would feel "reassured" that schools were providing children with a healthy diet.

But on plans for enforcement, he added: "None of us would consider ourselves experts in health and nutrition. Don't create another stick with which to beat head teachers when they are trying to do their very best to provide a healthy, balanced meal for those in our schools."

He said schools needed "more investment" in catering facilities and in the "professional development" of school chefs to develop menus that "meet the ambitions" of the government.

Schools Minister Georgia Gould told BBC Breakfast she was confident schools could deliver healthy meals within existing budgets, without diverting funding from elsewhere, like teaching, and that schools would be given a year to implement the changes.

She said the government was "absolutely determined to support schools" to redesign their menus affordably.

As part of the changes, deep-fried chips will have to be oven-baked instead, and pasta dishes will need to be 50% wholewheat once a week. High-fibre bread will also become a requirement.

Under the new rules, all dishes must come with at least one portion of fruit or vegetables

Breakfast clubs will undergo one of the biggest changes.

Historically, there has been no guidance on what they should provide, but from next September pastries and fried-eggs will be off the menu and there will be a sugar cap when it comes to cereals.

The government said Coco Pops would no longer be an option and chocolate spread was "not permitted".

Since February this year, 1,250 schools have offered free breakfast clubs to their pupils.

One of those was Oasis Academy Blakenhale in Birmingham, where principal Farzana Ahmed said the school welcomed the changes.

"The more children that can access a hot, nutritious meal, the better it is for us, the better it is for them, and actually it really supports families with the reduction of their financial pressures at home," she said.

Ahmed said it was "important" that schools are monitored, but added that they "probably need some more guidance from the government on what that's going to look like on a day-to-day basis".

Farzana Ahmed welcomed both the new school food standards and the expansion of free school meals eligibility

About 60% of pupils at the inner-city school receive free school meals, and Ahmed said they were already providing a healthy, balanced diet.

With free school meal eligibility expanding this year to all families who receive Universal Credit , Ahmed said there had been an "influx of parents" applying, and expects around 70% of pupils to benefit going forward.

"It's a really positive move," she said.

"We know how important a nutritional diet is to the wellbeing, to the behaviour, to the learning of our pupils."

This video can not be played

'My favourite is pizza' - Children give their views on school dinners

Working mum-of-three Kinza Butt said the free school meals her son was now getting at Blakenhale Juniors had lifted a "burden off the shoulders".

"He doesn't have to eat those cold sandwiches anymore," she said.

"By the end of the day he used to be starving. But now he's coming home all happy because he's having good, healthy meals with a snack as well."

Newly-eligible parent Kinza is delighted her children can now have free school dinners

The new food standards will apply to primary and secondary schools in England, but rules for school dinners vary across the UK.

In Wales, new guidance will come into force by the end of the year with a greater focus on at least two portions of vegetables being offered every day, with only water, milk or plant-based drinks allowed for hydration.

Scotland updated its legislation in 2020. It requires students to be offered at least two portions of vegetables and one portion of fruit every day and oily fish must be served at least once every three weeks.

Northern Ireland last updated its regulations in 2007. They include providing bread everyday, without spread, and offering two portions of fruit and vegetables a day. It also stipulates that if beans or pulses form the protein part of a main course, another vegetable must be available.
